---
title: "Detecting a rare variant"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")
```

```{r setup}
library(MMSpower)
```

Some surveillance questions are not about how common a variant is, but
whether it is there at all. A programme may want to know whether a new
drug-resistance mutation has arrived in a region, or whether *pfhrp2/3*
deletions are present before planning a full prevalence survey. The aim is
then to design a survey large enough that, if the variant is present at some low
prevalence, at least one case is very likely to be found.

`design_detection()` answers this. Given a full design instead, such as a
survey that has already been done, it returns `detection_prob`: how likely
that survey was to find the variant.

## Part 1: Designing the study

### How many samples?

Suppose the programme wants an 80% chance of finding at least one case if
the mutation is present in 1% of infections:

```{r}
d0 <- design_detection(prevalence = 0.01)
d0
```

So `r d0$n` samples are needed. The calculation is simple: each sample has
a 1% chance of being a case, so the chance of missing every case among $n$
samples is $(1 - 0.01)^n$, and $n$ is chosen to make that at most 20%.

The answer depends strongly on the target detection probability and on the
prevalence of the variant to be detected:

```{r}
design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, detection_prob = 0.95)$n
design_detection(prevalence = 0.005)$n
design_detection(prevalence = 0.02)$n
```

Raising the detection probability from 80% to 95% takes
`r design_detection(0.01, detection_prob = 0.95)$n` samples. Halving the
prevalence of the variant to 0.5% roughly doubles the sample size, and
doubling it to 2% roughly halves it. The plot shows the chance of finding at least one case
for different sample sizes:

```{r}
n_grid <- 1:600
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 1, 1), las = 1, bty = "l")
plot(n_grid, 1 - (1 - 0.01)^n_grid, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#1B2A41",
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Number of samples",
     ylab = "Chance of finding at least one case")
lines(n_grid, 1 - (1 - 0.005)^n_grid, lwd = 2, col = "#C0392B")
lines(n_grid, 1 - (1 - 0.02)^n_grid, lwd = 2, col = "#6B7280")
abline(h = 0.8, lty = 2, col = "#6B7280")
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2,
       col = c("#6B7280", "#1B2A41", "#C0392B"),
       legend = c("Prevalence 2%", "Prevalence 1%", "Prevalence 0.5%"))
```

To have an 80% chance of detecting at least one case, you would need
`r design_detection(prevalence = 0.02)$n` samples at a variant prevalence of
2%, `r d0$n` at 1%, and `r design_detection(prevalence = 0.005)$n` at 0.5%.

### An imperfect test

A case is only found if the test detects it. With a sensitivity of 90% and
a prevalence of 1%, each sample has a $0.01 \times 0.9$ chance of being a
detected case:

```{r}
d_test <- design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, sensitivity = 0.9)
d_test$n
```

The sample size rises from `r d0$n` to `r d_test$n`. Specificity is not
used: a positive result is assumed to be confirmed (for example by
sequencing) before the variant is declared present, so a false positive
does not count as finding a case.

### Clustering

Rare variants are often found in pockets: a new mutation may be common in
one district and absent from the next. In that case, testing many people at
one site mostly repeats what that site has already shown, and a survey
needs to reach many sites to find the variant. As in the other design
functions, this is described by the intra-cluster correlation (ICC). Here
we assume an ICC of 0.05.

**Fixing people per site.** If each site can collect 20 samples:

```{r}
d_per <- design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_per
```

The study needs `r d_per$n_sites` sites of `r d_per$n_per_site` people,
`r d_per$n` samples in total, compared with `r d0$n` with no clustering.

**Fixing the number of sites.** If the programme can visit 10 sites:

```{r}
d_sites <- design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, n_sites = 10, icc = 0.05)
d_sites
```

Each of the `r d_sites$n_sites` sites now needs `r d_sites$n_per_site`
people, `r d_sites$n` samples in total.

**More sites, fewer samples.** As for estimating prevalence, spreading the
samples over more sites reduces the total needed:

```{r}
d5  <- design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, n_sites = 5, icc = 0.05)
d20 <- design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, n_sites = 20, icc = 0.05)
c(sites_5 = d5$n, sites_10 = d_sites$n, sites_20 = d20$n)
```

Going from 5 to 20 sites cuts the total from `r d5$n` to `r d20$n`, closer
to the `r d0$n` an unclustered survey needs. Beyond that, adding sites
shrinks the people per site toward just a few, and because that number
rounds up to a whole person at every site, the total barely falls further.

With few sites and strong clustering, the numbers can become impractical.
With only 3 sites and an ICC of 0.3, the variant may simply be absent from
all three, and no practical number of people per site makes up for that:

```{r}
design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, n_sites = 3, icc = 0.3)$n_per_site
```

The answer is technically finite but far beyond any real survey. A fix is
to add more sites.

### Allowing for dropout and suspected cases

As with the other design functions, `design_detection()` gives the number
of samples needed **at analysis**. To reach it, inflate for expected losses
(withdrawn consent, lost or failed samples) and, if the variant is looked
for only in confirmed infections, for the share of suspected cases that are
confirmed. With 10% losses and 40% of suspected cases confirmed:

```{r}
n_analysis  <- d0$n
n_confirmed <- ceiling(n_analysis / (1 - 0.1))
n_suspected <- ceiling(n_confirmed / 0.4)
c(suspected = n_suspected, confirmed = n_confirmed, analysis = n_analysis)
```

So `r n_suspected` suspected cases are enrolled, `r n_confirmed` confirmed
cases are expected among them, and `r n_analysis` samples should reach the
analysis. Each step uses `ceiling()` to round up, since you cannot enrol
part of a person and rounding down would leave the study short. With sites,
do this per site rather than only for the total, so that every site still
delivers its share. The
[Estimating prevalence](tutorial-prevalence.html) tutorial works through
this in more detail, including confirmed fractions that differ by site.

## Part 2: Interpreting a survey that found nothing

Suppose 300 samples were
tested and no case of the mutation was found. How reassuring is that? Give
the full design, here `n = 300`, and the function returns `detection_prob`,
the chance that the survey would have found the variant if it were present
at 1%:

```{r}
r0 <- design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, n = 300)
r0$detection_prob
```

If the 300 samples were a simple random sample, there was a
`r round(100 * r0$detection_prob)`% chance of finding a 1% variant, so
finding none is good evidence that the prevalence is below 1%. But if the
300 samples came from clusters, for example 15 sites of 20 people, with an
ICC of 0.05:

```{r}
r_sites <- design_detection(prevalence = 0.01, n_sites = 15, n_per_site = 20,
                            icc = 0.05)
r_sites$detection_prob
```

the chance falls to `r round(100 * r_sites$detection_prob)`%. The same
number of negative results is weaker evidence when they come from clusters,
because a variant concentrated elsewhere could have been missed entirely.
When reporting that a variant was not found, state the prevalence it could
have been detected at, and with what chance.
